claims.claim: Eustathius of Antioch was a native of Side in Pamphylia.
Eustathius was bishop of Beroea around 320 and became patriarch/bishop of Antioch shortly before the Council of Nicaea in 325.
Eustathius died in exile at Trajanopolis in Thrace, probably about 337, though possibly as late as 370.
Eustathius was deposed by a synod at Antioch in 330 (or 327/331) for alleged Sabellianism and banished by Emperor Constantine the Great.
Jerome mentions that Eustathius composed several treatises against Arian doctrine, specifically mentioning De anima and De engastrimytho adversum Origenem.
The work De anima contra Arianos (also known as Contra Ariomanitas et de anima) was an anti-subordinationist treatise focusing on the soul, written against the Arians.
The work argued against Arian opponents who denied the human soul in the incarnated Logos, asserting that the Arians claimed the Logos assumed a human body without a human soul.
The work survives only in fragments and in an epitome compiled in the late fourth or early fifth century, preserved mainly in dogmatic florilegia.

The surviving fragments are found in Greek in Eulogius of Alexandria, the compiler of the Doctrina Patrum de incarnatione Verbi, and John Damascene; and in Latin in Facundus of Hermiane and Pope Gelasius.
The epitome offers significant new information about Arian Christology and presents a different view of early Arian thought compared to Athanasius's De incarnatione.
